Practicing on an owned lab target like DVWA or Metasploitable in BG Lab is the right way to learn about injection and how to detect it. On your own DVWA instance, run the union select that appends your own column names and see how the union returns rows you don't own. That's exactly the right way to build your understanding of how attackers probe for sensitive info and how to detect it in your own apps.

The setuid bit makes the binary execute with the file owner's privileges instead of the invoking user's — the classic case is a root-owned binary running as root. That's why setuid root binaries are privileged-escalation targets and must be audited.
A reverse shell is a shell that connects back from the target to the attacker's machine (outbound connection), which pierces inbound-firewall assumptions that bind a normal shell would violate.
Both SELECTs must return the same number of columns with compatible types — which is why attackers probe column count with ORDER BY n or NULL-padding, and why you can read the probe in your logs.

A CRC is an error-detection checksum: fast, and trivially forgeable because it isn't collision-resistant. A cryptographic hash (SHA-256) is designed so finding collisions or reversing it is infeasible — you use CRC for accidents and hashes for adversaries.

A CBC-mode padding oracle leaks information about the plaintext through its error responses (e.g., a 200 OK on a valid padding check, a 500 error on invalid padding). Attackers exploit this to decrypt ciphertexts bit by bit — every response reveals the value of one byte, and can be used to reconstruct the plaintext. DEFEND: verify the padding on the received ciphertext and report the result (success or failure) back to the attacker.

ASLR randomizes the memory layout (stack, heap, libraries) between runs, so an attacker can't hardcode return addresses — it raises the cost of buffer-overflow and ROP exploits, and is defeated by info-leaks that reveal addresses.

Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures: the behavior pattern of an adversary, not just an indicator. Tactics are the why (MITRE ATT&CK columns), techniques the how, procedures the specific implementation — every TTP is the complete execution of the adversary's strategy.

It wraps a string in single quotes and escapes embedded quotes so it becomes exactly one shell argument — user input can't introduce metacharacters. It's the fix for the command-injection class, paired with allowlist validation.

Since it's your own lab: low-security DVWA concatenates the id parameter straight into the query, so 1' union select user,password from users# closes the string and appends your SELECT. The dumped rows appear in the page — pair them with an offline MD5 crack. DEFEND: parameterized queries (PDO prepare with bound values) make the union unreachable; log id payloads containing quotes or UNION at the WAF.

Low security interpolates the ip parameter into a shell string: shell_exec('ping ' . $target). The semicolon is a shell metacharacter, so your command runs after ping inside the same shell. DEFEND: escapeshellarg() on the input, and log ip values containing shell metacharacters.

Use a prepared statement with bound parameters so user input is data, never SQL: PDO: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?'); $stmt->execute([$id]); Never interpolate variables into the SQL string. For dynamic clauses, whitelist column names against a fixed array.

Because it's a commonly used target for exploitation, default creds are a critical finding: they require zero exploit (authentication simply isn't enforced against them), and are often documented in the tool's own description. Default creds are a finding that highlights weak password-policy compliance and poor credential-management practice. In a real-world scenario, this would mean the vendor failed to enforce a strong password policy or failed to rotate at provisioning. DEFEND: rotate at provisioning and verify with a defaults checklist.

Look for: %27 or ' followed by union and select in the same parameter; %23 or -- terminators; unusually long id values; and response-size anomalies on 200s (dumped rows inflate the page). Alert on the pattern (union|select).*(from|information_schema) URL-decoded, then verify against parameterized-query coverage.

Look for: %27 or ' followed by shell metacharacters ( ;, |, `, $(), &&). The pattern is a bare shell argument followed by a shell command — every such occurrence is a failed attempt. DEFEND: escapeshellarg() plus allowlist validation like /^\$?\{.*\}$/ before it ever reaches a shell.

Sable-01 is the owned, offline cybersecurity LLM of the ScopeSable product house under BenchBrex — a fine-tuned local model that knows BenchBrex domain language, helps on owned lab targets, and enforces the refusal policy for anything targeting third parties. It exists for ownership and offline use, not to out-think frontier cloud models.
BeGuardit is the product house under BenchBrex that owns Sable-01 — the branded, owned cyber model. BenchBrex is the operating company; BeGuardit ships the productized AI.

BG Recon is the BeGuardit recon tool: an authorization-gated TCP port scanner with banner grab, plus a local posture audit — listeners with LAN-exposure flags, AI-runtime identification, and secrets-permission findings. Private-network targets by default; public targets need an explicit allow-external acknowledgment.

A fixed-scope review is BeGuardit's delivery model: an assessment with a defined boundary and roughly one-week duration — host config, services, secrets, AI runtime — producing findings, not an open-ended managed-service retainer.
